writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Minister for the Cabinet Office, what value of financial penalties her Department has imposed on Capita for contractual breaches in administering the Civil Service Pension Scheme.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Cabinet Office
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Cabinet Office awarded Capita the contract to administer the Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) in November 2023 under the previous government. The current delays facing scheme members are entirely unacceptable.

Out of the 12 contractually defined transition phases, multiple critical milestones have been missed, and the Government continues to hold Capita firmly to account using all commercial levers available, including withholding £9.9 million in contract payments, and will seek to recover all surge team costs directly from Capita. Though the Cabinet Office have not imposed financial penalties further to the amount withheld for failure to deliver, Capita have been making voluntary 10% deductions in their invoicing, pending commercial discussions. Further commercial, legal, and operational options remain on the table, and work is continuing on actively shaping a long-term strategy to bring this pension scheme back in-house.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, what assessment her Department has made of the potential implications for heritage conservation and local economic growth in Leicestershire of the addition of 58 sites in the Midlands to Historic England’s Heritage at Risk Register, published 5 November 2026; and what support her Department is providing to help local authorities prevent historic locations from falling into disrepair.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government recognises the importance of heritage conservation to local economies and communities across England, including in the Midlands. Historic England, the Department’s statutory adviser on the historic environment, monitors endangered sites through its annual Heritage at Risk Register to help identify priority assets. While 197 sites were added to the Register in 2026, 85 sites were successfully rescued and removed, demonstrating the tangible impact of the list in focusing conservation efforts and unlocking investment.

Custodians of heritage assets can access a range of dedicated government funding to support urgent repairs and bring historic buildings back into good use.This includes funding through the £230 million heritage investment package confirmed through to 2030 as part of the £1.5 billion Arts Everywhere Fund.

Most directly supporting assets on the Heritage at Risk Register, the Heritage at Risk Capital Fund is providing up to £60 million by 2030. This fund offers grants of up to £1 million to individuals and organisations legally responsible for conserving listed landmarks, registered gardens, and scheduled monuments. In October 2026, the Department announced that 23 heritage sites across England will receive over £23 million from this fund to protect and restore historic buildings that deliver the greatest benefit to communities in areas of highest need. Alongside this, the wider package includes £92 million through the Places of Worship Renewal Fund to support the repair of listed places of worship in areas of greatest need, and £42 million via the Heritage Revival Fund to support community-led regeneration.

Beyond these core funds, custodians can also apply for Historic England’s ongoing Repair Grants for Heritage at Risk and capacity-building support, as well as capital grant schemes administered by the National Lottery Heritage Fund.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Education, what steps her Department is taking to reduce the number of young people not in education, employment or training in South Shropshire.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Education
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The department recognises that supporting young people into education, employment or training is key to economic growth. This is a long-standing challenge requiring sustained reform. We are acting to strengthen pathways into education, employment and training and taking forward measures to prevent young people becoming not in education, employment or training (NEET), including earlier identification, stronger transition support and improved further education attendance.

In 2026, Shropshire reported that 3.6% of its 16 to 17-year-olds were NEET or not known. While this was up 0.6 percentage points from 2025, the rate remained below both the West Midlands rate of 5.7% and the England rate of 5.8%.

Shrewsbury College and Herefordshire, Ludlow and North Shropshire College are the main post-16 providers for South Shropshire, offering outreach and support for those at risk of disengagement. Recent investment in new science, technology, engineering and mathematics and construction facilities is increasing capacity and helping more young people remain engaged in education and training.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Energy Security and Net Zero, whether they have considered the merits of conducting (a) water and (b) energy impact assessments for data centres.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
writtenQuestions.answerText:
As set out in the Written Ministerial Statement on Enabling Sustainable Data Centre Growth Through Responsible Water and Energy Use, we are setting out a clear framework for sustainable data centre growth, while protecting water resources and electricity-system resilience. The approach combines transparency, efficient resource use, alternative water supplies, and stronger long-term planning.

Operators are encouraged to report annual water and energy metrics, including water usage effectiveness, power usage effectiveness, carbon disclosures, and electricity-system flexibility. Strategic data centres will have to report annually on their water and energy use, efficiency, emissions and heat reuse. Developers should minimise water demand, consider recycled sources before freshwater, assess waste-heat reuse, and evaluate location-specific water and energy risks.

All new data centres are encouraged to meet the Data Centre Covenant tests and demonstrate that they deliver tangible benefits for both the local area and the country. Data centres identified as strategically important and seeking enhanced government support will be required to meet these tests.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Work and Pensions, what steps he is taking to support entry-level employment opportunities in Wales.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department for Work and Pensions
writtenQuestions.answerText:
DWP supports entry-level employment opportunities in Wales through Jobcentre Plus, employer engagement, Work Hub and the JobHelp digital service, helping people prepare for work while supporting employers to fill vacancies through inclusive recruitment routes, work experience and apprenticeships.

DWP also utilises the likes of its Flexible Support Fund, to fund training, of industry specific licences to support citizens into local employment opportunities and reducing costs incurred the citizen and employers.

Young people are a key focus, with support available through the Youth Guarantee, including Youth Hubs, work experience opportunities, Youth Jobs Grant vacancies, Jobs Guarantee, and specialist provision such as Restart and Supported Recruitment Teams, helping young people gain the skills, confidence and experience needed to enter work.

DWP works closely with employers to create pathways into employment and remove barriers to recruitment. Through the Movement to Work Charity, DWP Wales has provided work experience placements to 260 young people this year in Wales, with a recent programme resulting in 43 job offers from 60 placements across Pembroke Dock, Wrexham and Ty Taf.

Wales is home to some of our strongest growth-driving sectors, from semiconductors to aerospace. Through the Industrial Strategy (IS) Job Plans led by the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade, the Government is partnering with business to ensure they have the right skills. IS Job Plans will help young people and adults access good jobs and progress in careers in sectors paying around £8,000 more than the national average.

DWP is also leading by example as an employer, creating 16 Executive Officer (EO) Social Mobility Apprenticeships through the Wales Skills Employment Pathway at Ty Taf, Treforest. DWP continues to work closely with the Welsh Government to align reserved employment support with devolved skills and employability provision

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, what assessment her Department has made of the adequacy of the accessibility of NHS trusts' approved clinical policies, procedures and patient-safety pathways to patients and the public.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care

answeringMember.name: Dame Diana Johnson
answeringMember.memberFrom: Kingston upon Hull North and Cottingham

writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Government recognises the importance of bereaved families being able to understand the care that was provided to their loved ones, and we are clear that families should be treated with compassion and supported to access relevant information, in a spirit of openness and transparency, subject to legal protections of confidential information.

NHS trusts are subject to the Freedom of Information Act 2000, including maintaining publication schemes under Section 19 of the Act, and providing reasonable advice and assistance under Section 16. The Information Commissioner’s Office provides independent guidance and oversight of these arrangements, and the Department continues to work with NHS England and relevant regulators to support transparency and information governance.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Health and Social Care, whether she has made an assessment of the adequacy of mortality data collection relating to energy drink consumption; and if she will consider reviewing how energy drinks are recorded on death certificates to improve understanding of their potential impact on serious illness and premature deaths.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Department of Health and Social Care

answeringMember.name: Dame Diana Johnson
answeringMember.memberFrom: Kingston upon Hull North and Cottingham

writtenQuestions.answerText:
In September 2025, the Government consulted on banning the sale of high-caffeine energy drinks to children, in light of the growing evidence linking energy drink consumption with a broad range of reported negative outcomes on children’s physical and mental health, and their education. Further information on those proposals, and the Government’s consideration of alternative approaches, including labelling requirements and public awareness campaigns, is set out in the consultation outcome published at the following link:

https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/banning-the-sale-of-high-caffeine-energy-drinks-to-children

A final impact assessment will be published on the GOV.UK website in due course, including its expected impacts on children, the food and drink industry, enforcement authorities, and the healthcare sector. No assessment has been made in relation to mortality data.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Affairs, what diplomatic and humanitarian action he has taken with regards to the political situation in South Sudan.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office
writtenQuestions.answerText: We continue to press South Sudan's leadership on the need for inclusive political dialogue as a necessary step towards peaceful, inclusive and credible elections. However, the elections scheduled for February will not in themselves complete South Sudan's transition: sustained inclusive political dialogue, security sector and public financial management reform, and accountability remain vital to a peaceful and prosperous future for South Sudan. As a leading donor, the UK is providing £72 million of aid to South Sudan this financial year, supporting humanitarian assistance, resilience and livelihoods, peacebuilding, health and education. This includes a £500,000 contribution to the World Health Organization to strengthen South Sudan's Ebola preparedness through improving surveillance, case detection and emergency response capacity. We continue to call on South Sudan's leadership to invest in its people.
writtenQuestions.heading: South Sudan: Politics and Government

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, what assessment his Department has made of the role of photonics in defence.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Defence
writtenQuestions.answerText:
The Ministry of Defence (MOD) has assessed photonics as an important enabling technology for modern defence capabilities, particularly in sensing, imaging, communications, targeting, navigation, weapons and quantum technologies.

Through the Defence Science and Technology Laboratory (Dstl), the MOD maintains oversight of developments across much of the photonics and quantum sectors, supports relevant research where it contributes to defence capability and, through the UK Complex Weapons Portfolio, research and development investment is supporting next-generation infra-red seeker and imaging technologies being developed by the expert UK industry supply base.

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, what steps his Department is taking to strengthen the Royal Navy's capability to protect UK territorial waters and critical national infrastructure from emerging maritime threats.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Defence
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Following the Strategic Defence Review, the Royal Navy is strengthening its ability to protect critical undersea infrastructure through Atlantic Bastion and the development of the Hybrid Navy. This will integrate existing ships, submarines and aircraft with autonomous underwater, surface and airborne systems, supported by the Maritime Fighting Web, to increase the Fleet’s reach, persistence and resilience.

The Defence Investment Plan commits an additional £330 million for critical underwater infrastructure protection capabilities, including enhancements to RFA Proteus. A further £260 million was allocated to upgrade Royal Air Force P-8A Poseidon Maritime Patrol Aircraft and equip it with the UK-built Stingray torpedo.
writtenQuestions.heading: Navy: National Security

writtenQuestions.questionText: To ask the Secretary of State for Defence, how many major exercises in the last 12 months have tested mobilisation at scale.
writtenQuestions.answeringBodyName: Ministry of Defence
writtenQuestions.answerText:
Over the last 12 months, the Ministry of Defence has routinely conducted and participated in a wide range of exercises of varying scale to test military readiness, mobilisation, resilience and interoperability with Allies. This included Exercise HEDGEHOG which tested mobilisation at scale and incorporated novel deployment and civilian capabilities to employ a force into Northern Europe by road, rail and air in a two day period.

Looking ahead to next year, the Ministry of Defence will participate in the NATO Crisis Management Exercise 2027, ALBISTON SHADOW and STEADFAST DEFENDER 2027, which, whilst separate exercises, aim to test Alliance consultation and decision-making, military mobilisation, national resilience and preparedness. These activities are complemented by wider planning and exercising, which helps ensure Defence’s mobilisation and readiness arrangements are fully integrated with broader national resilience and preparedness efforts across Government.
